areas.name: Precision Agriculture
areas.title: Precision Agriculture
areas.metaDescription: Label-efficient computer vision for precision agriculture: wheat head detection and segmentation, Fusarium damaged kernel phenotyping, synthetic data generation, and video object segmentation in dense crop canopies.
intro: Deep learning for crop phenotyping is limited less by model capacity than by annotation cost. Field images of cereal canopies contain hundreds of small, densely packed, self-occluded objects per frame, and pixel-accurate labels for those objects are slow and expensive to produce. Most of my precision agriculture research asks the same question in different forms: how far can a high-performing vision model be pushed when only a handful of human-annotated images exist?

The answer developed across these papers is a family of semi-self-supervised pipelines. A small number of manually annotated images is used to synthesize a large computationally annotated dataset, either by cut-and-paste composition, by generative models such as CycleGAN and denoising diffusion, or by procedural plant models built with L-systems and rendered in a game engine. A model trained on that synthetic data is then moved toward the real data distribution through staged domain adaptation, strong augmentation, and pseudo-labeling with student-teacher refinement.

The tasks span object detection, semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and video object segmentation, and the crops and sensing setups vary from handheld video to drone flights to controlled seed-belt imaging. Alongside the methods, this work contributes public benchmark data: the WheatSeedBelt single-kernel damage dataset, and, through the Global Wheat Dataset Consortium, the GWFSS wheat organ segmentation dataset.

areas.name: Precision Health
areas.title: Precision Health
areas.metaDescription: Machine learning and medical image analysis for precision health: noninvasive MRI biomarkers, histopathological diagnosis, kidney disease progression, and model development practice for small clinical datasets.
intro: In clinical imaging the constraint is different from agriculture but structurally similar: the ground truth is scarce, expensive, and sometimes obtainable only through an invasive procedure. My precision health research builds models that recover clinically meaningful information from images already acquired as part of standard care, so that a decision can be informed before treatment rather than after surgery.

The work spans three imaging scales. On brain MRI, radiomic features from the peritumoral edema predict how a metastasis is invading the surrounding parenchyma, something an expert neuroradiologist cannot reliably read. On kidney MRI, image features fused with clinical variables identify which patients with polycystic kidney disease will lose function fastest. On histopathology slides, a synthesis pipeline recomposes tissue segments into many training examples so that a celiac disease classifier can be trained from a few hundred biopsies rather than a few thousand.

Running through all of it is the same methodological discipline, set out in the machine learning review written for Neuroimaging Clinics of North America: patient-wise splits to prevent leakage, feature selection performed only on training data, standardization across scanners, ensembling across models, and evaluation on held-out test sets. Small clinical datasets punish shortcuts, and most of the effort goes into not taking them.

This research is carried out with the Augmented Intelligence and Precision Health Laboratory at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre and the Radiomics and Augmented Intelligence Laboratory at the University of Florida College of Medicine.

publications.title: A Semi-Self-Supervised Learning Approach for Wheat Head Detection Using Extremely Small Number of Labeled Samples
publications.shortTitle: Wheat head detection from very few labels
publications.venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision Workshops (ICCVW), CVPPA
publications.summary: Trains a wheat head detector from three contoured images and a few minutes of handheld video. The annotated wheat heads are cut out, augmented, and pasted onto background field footage to simulate a large computationally annotated dataset, and two domain adaptation stages then close the gap to real imagery.
publications.abstract: Most of the success of deep learning is owed to supervised learning, where a large-scale annotated dataset is used for model training. However, developing such datasets is challenging. In this paper, we develop a semi-self-supervised learning approach for wheat head detection. The proposed method utilized a few short video clips and only one annotated image from each video clip of wheat fields to simulate a large computationally annotated dataset used for model building. Considering the domain gap between the simulated and real images, we applied two domain adaptation steps to alleviate the challenge of distributional shift. The resulting model achieved high performance when applied to real unannotated datasets. When fine-tuned on the dataset from the Global Wheat Head Detection Challenge, the performance was further improved. The model achieved a mean average precision of 0.827, where an overlap of 50% or more between a predicted bounding box and ground truth was considered as a correct prediction. Although the utility of the proposed methodology was shown by applying it to wheat head detection, the proposed method is not limited to this application and could be used for other domains, such as detecting different crop types, alleviating the barrier of lack of large-scale annotated datasets in those domains.
contributions: Introduces a semi-self-supervised pipeline that generates labeled training data for the target task itself, rather than for an unrelated pretext task.
Uses short video clips of wheat fields and of empty background scenes as the raw data source, making data collection nearly free compared with building an annotated image dataset.
Applies two sequential domain adaptation stages: strong augmentation of rotated representative images, then pseudo-labeling of real unannotated video frames.
Reaches mAP@50 of 0.827 after fine-tuning on the Global Wheat Head Detection dataset, above the 0.741 supervised baseline trained on the same dataset.
methods: YOLO object detection with CIoU loss
data: 3 wheat field video clips and 17 background video clips (roughly 11 and 41 minutes)
294,511 extracted background frames; 17,979 wheat field frames; 3 contoured representative images
36,000 computationally annotated synthetic samples
Global Wheat Head Detection (GWHD) 2021 dataset, 1,381-image test subset
results: mAP@50 of 0.090 from synthetic data alone, exposing the domain gap
mAP@50 of 0.601 after both domain adaptation stages without seeing GWHD
mAP@50 of 0.827 after GWHD fine-tuning, versus 0.741 for the supervised baseline
applications: Wheat yield component estimation and spike counting
High-throughput plant phenotyping for breeding programs
Bootstrapping annotation for other crops and dense-object domains

publications.title: Semi-Self-Supervised Learning for Semantic Segmentation in Images with Dense Patterns
publications.summary: Extends the synthesis-plus-domain-adaptation idea from detection to pixel-level segmentation. Two annotated images and one short video clip are enough to train a customized U-Net that reaches a Dice score of 0.89 internally and generalizes to wheat fields from 18 domains across five countries.
publications.abstract: Deep learning has shown potential in domains with large-scale annotated datasets. However, manual annotation is expensive, time-consuming, and tedious. Pixel-level annotations are particularly costly for semantic segmentation in images with dense irregular patterns of object instances, such as in plant images. In this work, we propose a method for developing high-performing deep learning models for semantic segmentation of such images utilizing little manual annotation. As a use case, we focus on wheat head segmentation. We synthesize a computationally annotated dataset - using a few annotated images, a short unannotated video clip of a wheat field, and several video clips with no wheat - to train a customized U-Net model. Considering the distribution shift between the synthesized and real images, we apply three domain adaptation steps to gradually bridge the domain gap. Only using two annotated images, we achieved a Dice score of 0.89 on the internal test set. When further evaluated on a diverse external dataset collected from 18 different domains across five countries, this model achieved a Dice score of 0.73.
contributions: Adapts semi-self-supervised data synthesis from bounding-box detection to pixel-level semantic segmentation of dense irregular object patterns.
Uses a three-step domain adaptation schedule to move a model trained on synthetic composites toward real field imagery.
Demonstrates cross-country, cross-domain generalization by evaluating on wheat imagery from 18 distinct domains in five countries.
Shows that two manually annotated images can support a segmentation model competitive with supervised training.
data: Two manually annotated wheat field images
One short unannotated wheat field video clip and several no-wheat background clips
External evaluation set spanning 18 domains across five countries
results: Dice score 0.89 on the internal test set using only two annotated images
Dice score 0.73 on the diverse external multi-domain test set
applications: Wheat head area and density estimation
Field phenomics and breeding trial analysis
Any segmentation task with dense, self-occluding, repeating object instances

publications.title: Detection of Fusarium Damaged Kernels in Wheat Using Deep Semi-Supervised Learning on a Novel WheatSeedBelt Dataset
publications.venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision Workshops (ICCVW)
publications.summary: Introduces WheatSeedBelt, a 40,420-image single-kernel dataset covering 268 wheat varieties with damage annotations, and uses it to train semi-supervised classifiers for Fusarium damaged kernel grading. An inter-rater study shows human experts do not outperform the model.
publications.abstract: Fusarium head blight, caused by Fusarium spp., is a destructive disease of wheat worldwide. Fusarium damaged kernels (FDKs) significantly reduce grain yield and quality. Thus, FDK detection is a priority for wheat breeders seeking to develop high-grain quality and FDK-resistant wheat cultivars. However, traditional FDK measurement methods are time-consuming, labor-intensive, and of variable accuracy. Image-based phenotyping methods have the potential to efficiently detect FDK, but are challenging to develop due to the lack of large-scale damage-annotated wheat kernel datasets. Addressing this issue, we introduced WheatSeedBelt, a high-resolution large-scale dataset including 40,420 close-up top- and side-view single-kernel images of 268 wheat varieties with kernel damage annotations. Utilizing this dataset, we developed an image-processing pipeline to efficiently process images and extract the representative features for machine and deep-learning purposes. We also conducted three experiments on the dataset using pretraining and semi-supervised fine-tuning phases to classify wheat kernels into healthy, unhealthy but non-FDK, and FDK affected. Our best models achieved an F1-score of 84.29% for the Healthy-Unhealthy (including FDKs) task, 56.35% for the binary FDK-nonFDK, and 68.30% for the 3-class task (Healthy, Unhealthy, and FDK). We also conducted an inter-rater reliability study, which indicated that human experts do not outperform our model in FDK prediction, providing evidence that visual classification of FDK from RGB images is a challenging task.
contributions: Releases WheatSeedBelt, a large-scale annotated single-kernel wheat imaging dataset built on a seed belt imaging setup.
Provides an image-processing pipeline for kernel isolation and representative feature extraction from belt imagery.
Evaluates pretraining followed by semi-supervised fine-tuning across binary and three-class damage grading tasks.
Quantifies the ceiling of the task through an inter-rater reliability study with human experts.
data: WheatSeedBelt: 40,420 top- and side-view single-kernel images
268 wheat varieties with kernel damage annotations
results: F1-score 84.29% for the healthy versus unhealthy task
F1-score 68.30% for the three-class healthy / unhealthy / FDK task
F1-score 56.35% for the binary FDK versus non-FDK task
Human experts did not outperform the model on FDK prediction
applications: Fusarium head blight resistance screening in wheat breeding
Grain quality and food safety grading
Automated seed phenotyping on belt imaging systems

publications.title: Efficient Wheat Head Segmentation with Minimal Annotation: A Generative Approach
publications.venue: Journal of Imaging, volume 10, issue 7, article 152
publications.summary: Closes the simulation-to-reality gap with a modified CycleGAN. A large computationally simulated annotated dataset is translated into realistic field imagery, and the resulting model is refined through pseudo-labeling without additional manual annotation.
publications.abstract: Deep learning models have been used for a variety of image processing tasks. However, most of these models are developed through supervised learning approaches, which rely heavily on the availability of large-scale annotated datasets. Developing such datasets is tedious and expensive. In the absence of an annotated dataset, synthetic data can be used for model development; however, due to the substantial differences between simulated and real data, a phenomenon referred to as domain gap, the resulting models often underperform when applied to real data. In this research, we aim to address this challenge by first computationally simulating a large-scale annotated dataset and then using a generative adversarial network (GAN) to fill the gap between simulated and real images.
contributions: Adapts CycleGAN so that image translation preserves the geometry required for the paired segmentation masks to stay valid.
Combines computational simulation, unpaired image translation, and pseudo-label fine-tuning into one annotation-free pipeline.
Demonstrates that generative domain translation improves over training on raw simulated data.
data: Computationally simulated annotated wheat field images
Real unannotated wheat field imagery
applications: Annotation-free segmentation model development for crops
Synthetic-to-real transfer in agricultural imaging

publications.title: SynthSet: Generative Diffusion Model for Semantic Segmentation in Precision Agriculture
publications.venue: Computer Vision - ECCV 2024 Workshops, Lecture Notes in Computer Science volume 15625
publications.summary: Generates image and mask pairs from noise. A dual diffusion architecture synthesizes agricultural imagery together with its own pixel-level annotation, with no human labeling at any stage, and super-resolution sharpens the phenotypic detail and image-mask coherence.
publications.abstract: This paper introduces a methodology for generating synthetic annotated data to address data scarcity in semantic segmentation tasks within the precision agriculture domain. Utilizing Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), we propose a dual diffusion model architecture for synthesizing realistic annotated agricultural data, without any human intervention. We employ super-resolution to enhance the phenotypic characteristics of the synthesized images and their coherence with the corresponding generated masks. We showcase the utility of the proposed method for wheat head segmentation. The high quality of synthesized data underscores the effectiveness of the proposed methodology in generating image-mask pairs. Furthermore, models trained on our generated data exhibit promising performance when tested on an external, diverse dataset of real wheat fields.
contributions: Proposes a dual diffusion architecture that generates an image and its segmentation mask jointly rather than labeling generated images afterwards.
Removes human intervention entirely from the training data creation loop.
Adds a super-resolution stage to improve fine phenotypic structure and image-mask alignment.
Validates the synthetic data by training segmentation models and testing on external real wheat field imagery.
data: Fully synthetic wheat image and mask pairs generated by the model
External diverse real wheat field dataset used for evaluation
applications: Training data generation where annotation is infeasible
Benchmark augmentation for crop segmentation models
Transferable synthesis methodology for other dense-canopy crops

publications.title: Beyond Annotations: Efficient Wheat Head Segmentation Using L-Systems, Game Engines, and Student-Teacher Models
publications.venue: Computer Vision - ECCV 2024 Workshops, Lecture Notes in Computer Science volume 15625
publications.summary: Builds the training set from a plant growth model instead of from photographs. Lindenmayer systems describe wheat morphology, a game engine renders the scenes with perfect masks, and a student-teacher loop adapts the resulting model to real fields, reaching a Dice score of 0.87 with no manual annotation.
publications.abstract: The increasing global population necessitates efficient monitoring of wheat fields to ensure food security. Traditional manual methods for crop monitoring are labor-intensive and inefficient, hindering the adoption of precision agriculture techniques. Deep learning-based semantic segmentation has shown promise in tasks such as yield prediction, crop health monitoring, and disease detection. However, the creation of large-scale annotated datasets required for training these models is resource-intensive. This paper proposes a self-supervised approach for wheat head segmentation, leveraging Lindenmayer systems (L-systems) to generate a synthetic dataset and employing a student-teacher model for domain adaptation. The methodology involves training a semantic segmentation model on synthetic data and refining it with pseudo-labeled real data. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation performance, achieving a Dice score of 0.87, setting a new benchmark in wheat head segmentation without requiring manual annotation.
contributions: Uses procedural plant modeling with L-systems to encode wheat morphology rather than sampling it from photographs.
Renders synthetic scenes in a game engine, which yields pixel-perfect masks for free.
Applies student-teacher domain adaptation with pseudo-labeled real imagery.
Achieves a Dice score of 0.87 with no manual annotation.
data: Procedurally generated synthetic wheat scenes with exact segmentation masks
Real unannotated wheat field imagery for pseudo-labeling
results: Dice score of 0.87 without any manual annotation
applications: Crop health monitoring and yield prediction
Simulation-driven training for agricultural vision systems
Procedural data generation for other plant species

publications.title: A Semi-Self-Supervised Approach for Dense-Pattern Video Object Segmentation
publications.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
publications.summary: Extends dense-pattern segmentation from still images to video. Synthetic clips that mimic real camera and object motion are used for pretraining, then pseudo-labeled real video refines the model, which holds up on drone footage across growth stages from boot stage to harvest.
publications.abstract: Video object segmentation (VOS), predicting pixel-level regions for objects within each frame of a video, is particularly challenging in agricultural scenarios, where videos of crops include hundreds of small, dense, and occluded objects (stems, leaves, flowers, pods) that sway and move unpredictably in the wind. Supervised training is the state-of-the-art for VOS, but it requires large, pixel-accurate, human-annotated videos, which are costly to produce for videos with many densely packed objects in each frame. We train the model first with synthetic data that mimics the camera and object motion of real videos and then with pseudo-labeled videos. We evaluate our DVOS method for wheat head segmentation from a diverse set of videos (handheld, drone-captured, different field locations, and different growth stages, spanning from boot stage to wheat mature and harvest ready). Despite using only a few manually annotated video frames, the proposed approach yielded a high-performing model, achieving a Dice score of 0.79 when tested on a drone-captured external test set. While our method was evaluated on wheat head segmentation, it can be extended to other crops and domains, such as crowd analysis or microscopic image analysis.
contributions: Defines dense video object segmentation (DVOS) as a distinct problem: hundreds of small, occluded, wind-moved objects per frame.
Synthesizes training video that reproduces both camera motion and object motion, not just static appearance.
Uses pseudo-labeled real video as the second training stage, requiring only a few annotated frames.
Validates across handheld and drone capture, multiple field locations, and growth stages from boot stage to harvest.
methods: Synthetic video generation with motion simulation
Diffusion-based and temporal modeling of frame sequences
data: Handheld and drone-captured wheat field video
Multiple field locations and growth stages (boot stage through harvest ready)
A small number of manually annotated video frames
results: Dice score of 0.79 on a drone-captured external test set
applications: Drone and handheld crop monitoring over time
Temporal plant phenotyping and growth-stage tracking
Transferable to crowd analysis and microscopy with similar density characteristics

publications.title: From Semantic To Instance: A Semi-Self-Supervised Learning Approach
publications.summary: Introduces GLMask, an image-mask representation that pushes the model toward shape, texture, and pattern rather than color, and a pipeline that converts semantic segmentation into instance segmentation. Reaches mAP@50 of 98.5% on wheat head instance segmentation and improves COCO by over 12.6 mAP@50.
publications.abstract: Instance segmentation is essential for applications such as automated monitoring of plant health, growth, and yield. However, extensive effort is required to create large-scale datasets with pixel-level annotations of each object instance for developing instance segmentation models that restrict the use of deep learning in these areas. This challenge is more significant in images with densely packed, self-occluded objects, which are common in agriculture. To address this challenge, we propose a semi-self-supervised learning approach that requires minimal manual annotation to develop a high-performing instance segmentation model. We design GLMask, an image-mask representation for the model to focus on shape, texture, and pattern while minimizing its dependence on color features. We develop a pipeline to generate semantic segmentation and then transform it into instance-level segmentation. The proposed approach substantially outperforms the conventional instance segmentation models, establishing a state-of-the-art wheat head instance segmentation model with mAP@50 of 98.5%. Additionally, we assessed the proposed methodology on the general-purpose Microsoft COCO dataset, achieving a significant performance improvement of over 12.6% mAP@50. This highlights that the utility of our proposed approach extends beyond precision agriculture and applies to other domains, specifically those with similar data characteristics.
contributions: Designs GLMask, an image-mask representation that reduces the model's reliance on color and emphasizes shape, texture, and pattern.
Provides a pipeline that lifts semantic segmentation output into instance-level segmentation without instance-level annotation.
Sets a state-of-the-art wheat head instance segmentation result at mAP@50 of 98.5%.
Shows the method generalizes beyond agriculture with an improvement of over 12.6 mAP@50 on Microsoft COCO.
data: Wheat head imagery with densely packed, self-occluded instances
Microsoft COCO for general-purpose validation
results: mAP@50 of 98.5% for wheat head instance segmentation
Over 12.6% mAP@50 improvement on Microsoft COCO
applications: Per-plant and per-organ counting for yield estimation
Automated plant health and growth monitoring
Instance segmentation in any densely packed, self-occluded domain

publications.title: The Global Wheat Full Semantic Organ Segmentation (GWFSS) Dataset
publications.summary: The Global Wheat Dataset Consortium's successor to GWHD. Where GWHD provided bounding boxes for wheat heads, GWFSS provides full semantic segmentation of leaves, stems, and spikes across all developmental stages, assembled from 11 institutions and many different imaging setups.
publications.abstract: Computer vision is increasingly used in farmers' fields and agricultural experiments to quantify important traits. Imaging setups with a sub-millimeter ground sampling distance enable the detection and tracking of plant features, including size, shape, and colour. Although today's AI-driven foundation models segment almost any object in an image, they still fail for complex plant canopies. To improve model performance, the global wheat dataset consortium assembled a diverse set of images from experiments around the globe. After the head detection dataset (GWHD), the new dataset targets a full semantic segmentation (GWFSS) of organs (leaves, stems and spikes) covering all developmental stages. Images were collected by 11 institutions using a wide range of imaging setups.
contributions: Extends the Global Wheat Dataset Consortium benchmark from head detection to full organ-level semantic segmentation.
Covers leaves, stems, and spikes across all wheat developmental stages.
Aggregates imagery from 11 institutions with heterogeneous imaging setups, making domain diversity part of the benchmark.
Ships a labelled subset of 1,096 ground-truth images alongside a larger unlabelled set, released through the ETH Research Collection.

Images from 11 institutions across multiple countries and imaging setups
Hosted in the ETH Research Collection (doi:10.3929/ethz-b-000734546)
applications: Benchmarking segmentation foundation models on complex plant canopies
Trait extraction for wheat breeding and crop management
Cross-domain generalization studies in field phenomics

publications.title: Machine learning prediction of brain metastasis invasion pattern on brain magnetic resonance imaging scans
publications.shortTitle: Brain metastasis invasion pattern from MRI
publications.authorNote: Keyhan Najafian and Benjamin Rehany contributed equally.
publications.venue: Neuro-Oncology Advances, volume 6, issue 1, article vdae200
publications.summary: Brain metastasis invasion pattern is prognostic but can currently only be read from resected tissue. This study shows it can be predicted from preoperative MRI with 85% accuracy, using radiomic features from the peritumoral edema, in a task where expert neuroradiologists reach only 44 to 59%.
publications.abstract: Background. Brain metastasis invasion pattern (BMIP) is an emerging biomarker associated with recurrence-free and overall survival in patients, and differential response to therapy in preclinical models. Currently, BMIP can only be determined from the histopathological examination of surgical specimens, precluding its use as a biomarker prior to therapy initiation. The aim of this study was to investigate the potential of machine learning (ML) approaches to develop a noninvasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based biomarker for BMIP determination. Methods. From an initial cohort of 329 patients, a subset of 132 patients met the inclusion criteria for this retrospective study. We evaluated the ability of an expert neuroradiologist to reliably predict BMIP. Thereafter, the dataset was randomly divided into training/validation (80% of cases) and test subsets (20% of cases). The ground truth for BMIP was the histopathologic evaluation of resected specimens. Following MRI sequence co-registration, advanced feature extraction techniques deriving hand-crafted radiomic features with traditional ML classifiers and convolution-based deep learning (CDL) models were trained and evaluated. Different ML approaches were used individually or using ensembling techniques to determine the model with the best performance for BMIP prediction. Results. Expert evaluation of brain MRI scans could not reliably predict BMIP, with an accuracy of 44% to 59% depending on the semantic feature used. Among the different ML and CDL models evaluated, the best-performing model achieved an accuracy of 85% and an F1 score of 90%. Conclusions. ML approaches can effectively predict BMIP, representing a noninvasive MRI-based approach to guide the management of patients with brain metastases.
contributions: First study to predict brain metastasis invasion pattern noninvasively from MRI using radiomics and machine learning.
Shows that conventional semantic imaging features read by an expert neuroradiologist do not reliably predict invasion pattern.
Finds that the peritumoral edema region on T2-weighted images, not the enhancing tumor itself, carries the most predictive signal.
Uses patient-wise splits, training-only feature selection, and image-level standardization across two scanners to guard against leakage and scanner bias.
methods: Support vector classifier, random forest, multi-layer perceptron
Variance filtering and chi-square feature selection
data: 329 screened patients, 132 eligible for machine learning analysis
Preoperative T2-weighted and post-contrast T1-weighted MRI acquired on 3.0 T Philips and 1.5 T GE Signa scanners
Histopathological invasion scoring by two blinded observers as ground truth
Source numerical data available on reasonable request; patient images cannot be shared for privacy reasons
results: Best ensemble model: 85% accuracy, 93% precision, 87% recall, 90% F1 score
Peritumoral edema features outperformed enhancing tumor features by roughly 18%
Expert neuroradiologist accuracy ranged from 44.2% to 59.0% across semantic features
Inter-observer agreement for histopathological scoring: 83.7%, Cohen's kappa 0.66

publications.title: A Deep Learning-Based Pipeline for Celiac Disease Diagnosis Using Histopathological Images
publications.venue: Computer Analysis of Images and Patterns (CAIP 2021), Lecture Notes in Computer Science volume 13052
publications.summary: Diagnoses celiac disease from whole slide images of duodenal biopsies using far fewer slides than a conventional pipeline needs. An Image Assembler synthesizes training examples by recomposing tissue segments onto a blank canvas, and patient-level predictions come from a majority vote across 101 synthesized images.
publications.abstract: With an increasing number of celiac disease diagnoses and the increasing number of misdiagnoses, automated approaches are valuable to aid pathologists in efficiently diagnosing this disease. Histopathological analysis of intestinal biopsy is considered the gold standard for diagnosis. Convolutional neural networks have achieved promising results for various image processing tasks. A common challenge in medical imaging analysis is obtaining a large number of samples, impeding the full potential of deep learning. In this paper, we propose a classification pipeline to train deep convolutional neural networks to accurately diagnosis celiac disease using models trained with a small number of samples. To show the utility of this approach, we compared it to a typical classification pipeline. The results indicate the superiority of our classification pipeline in distinguishing celiac disease from normal tissue with precision, recall, and accuracy of 0.941, 0.889, and 0.893, respectively. Although we showed the utility of the proposed pipeline for celiac diagnosis, it can also be used for other applications utilizing histopathological imaging.
contributions: Introduces Image Assembler, which segments tissue from a whole slide image and recomposes random subsets of segments onto a blank canvas to synthesize many labeled training examples per patient.
Aggregates the many per-slide predictions into one patient-level diagnosis through a majority vote, avoiding the mislabeling risk of patch-level training.
Shows that composing four segments per synthetic image outperforms both single segments and whole slide images on every metric.
Provides a pipeline that is independent of the underlying architecture and transferable to other whole slide pathology classification tasks.
data: 426 digitized duodenal biopsy slides from the McGill University Health Centre Department of Pathology, 2016 to 2019
Slides graded by Marsh histotype; ambiguous histotype 2 cases excluded
174 normal and 247 diseased samples after grouping
Patient-wise split of 60% training, 20% validation, 20% testing

publications.title: Overview of Machine Learning Part 1: Fundamentals and Classic Approaches
publications.shortTitle: Machine learning fundamentals for medical imaging
publications.venue: Neuroimaging Clinics of North America, volume 30, issue 4, pages e17-e32
publications.summary: A review written for clinicians and imaging researchers, covering classic supervised and unsupervised machine learning, the full predictive modeling workflow, and the practices that decide whether a model generalizes. Written around the constraint that defines medical datasets: small sample sizes and missing values.
publications.abstract: As health data and computer power become increasingly available, the main challenge is to gain actionable insight from these data. Machine learning methods have proved to be a viable approach for mining valuable insight from data across various fields. This article provides an overview of the classic supervised and unsupervised machine learning methods as well as fundamental concepts required for understanding how to develop generalizable and high-performance machine learning applications. It also describes the important steps for developing a machine learning model and how decisions made in these steps affect model performance and ability to generalize. Key points: small sample sizes and missing values are two common characteristics of medical datasets that make developing predictive models challenging; classic machine learning methods can be used to build predictive models using small datasets; developing a machine learning application requires following a workflow including data acquisition, exploratory data analysis, data cleaning, dimensionality reduction, model building and validation, and model evaluation; understanding model complexity, variance, and bias is required for the successful application of machine learning; and following best practices for model evaluation is necessary for developing generalizable models.
contributions: Lays out the end-to-end predictive modeling workflow: data acquisition, exploratory analysis, cleaning, dimensionality reduction, training and validation, and evaluation.
Explains the bias-variance tradeoff and its relationship to model complexity in terms usable by clinical researchers.
Covers class imbalance, a defining feature of health data, and the tradeoffs of oversampling against undersampling.
Sets out evaluation practice: held-out test sets, nested cross-validation, and choosing performance measures that reflect the clinical question.
methods: Support vector machines and the kernel trick
Feature selection: filter, wrapper, and embedded methods
applications: Teaching machine learning method selection to radiologists and clinical researchers
Model development practice for small medical datasets
Reference for evaluation and validation design in clinical machine learning

publications.title: Using Deep Learning to Determine Kidney Function Decline in Patients with ADPKD
publications.venue: Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, volume 34, issue 11S, page 406
publications.summary: Predicts which patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease will lose kidney function rapidly, by fusing MRI features with clinical variables rather than relying on height-adjusted total kidney volume alone.
publications.abstract: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is associated with progressive kidney cyst growth, eventually leading to kidney failure in many patients. The current risk stratification tool uses height-adjusted total kidney volume (TKV) by age. However, it does not include clinical or other imaging features that may contribute to kidney function decline. In this study, we developed a deep learning classifier that integrates clinical and imaging features to predict rapid estimated GFR (eGFR) decline in patients with ADPKD. We included 120 patients with confirmed ADPKD with at least one MRI scan and at least 3 serial eGFR measures. An eGFR decline of 4 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year or greater was defined as rapid progression. We tripled the sample size by extracting the largest manually segmented 2D MRI slice and its two neighbouring slices for each patient. Pixel-level and spatial-level transformations were applied to the images to enhance our deep model's generalizability and robustness. The model consisted of three components: EfficientNet-b2, FuseNet, and a classifier, with a train:validation:test split of 63:17:20. The EfficientNet-b2 extracted 1000 features from each MRI slice. The FuseNet performed feature fusion on 15 clinically relevant features associated with ADPKD. The feature maps obtained from both models were concatenated and fed into the classifier. Weighted-average F1 and AUC scores and the confusion matrix were used to assess the model's performance.
contributions: Combines imaging and clinical information rather than relying on height-adjusted total kidney volume by age, the current risk stratification standard.
Fuses 1000 image features from EfficientNet-b2 with 15 clinically relevant ADPKD variables through a dedicated fusion network.
Expands a small cohort by using the largest segmented slice and its two neighbours per patient, with pixel-level and spatial-level augmentation.
data: 120 patients with confirmed ADPKD, each with at least one MRI scan and at least three serial eGFR measures
Rapid progression defined as eGFR decline of 4 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year or greater
Manually segmented 2D MRI slices plus two neighbouring slices per patient
Train, validation, and test split of 63:17:20
applications: Risk stratification of ADPKD patients before kidney failure
Multimodal prognostic modeling in nephrology
Earlier identification of candidates for intervention

publications.title: Predicting phenotypes from novel genomic markers using deep learning
publications.venue: Bioinformatics Advances, volume 3, issue 1, article vbad028
publications.summary: Genomic selection usually runs on SNP markers. This work shows that structural variants and transposable elements predict crop phenotypes better, using NovGMDeep, a 1D convolutional network evaluated on Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa.
publications.abstract: Genomic selection (GS) models use single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers to predict phenotypes. However, these predictive models face challenges due to the high dimensionality of genome-wide SNP marker data. Thanks to recent breakthroughs in DNA sequencing and decreased sequencing cost, the study of novel genomic variants such as structural variations (SVs) and transposable elements (TEs) become increasingly prevalent. In this article, we develop a deep convolutional neural network model, NovGMDeep, to predict phenotypes using SVs and TEs markers for GS. The proposed model is trained and tested on samples of Arabidopsis thaliana and Oryza sativa using k-fold cross-validation. The prediction accuracy is evaluated using Pearson's Correlation Coefficient (PCC), mean absolute error (MAE) and SD of MAE. The predicted results showed higher correlation when the model is trained with SVs and TEs than with SNPs. NovGMDeep also has higher prediction accuracy when comparing with conventional statistical models. This work sheds light on the unappreciated function of SVs and TEs in genotype-to-phenotype associations, as well as their extensive significance and value in crop development.
contributions: Moves genomic selection beyond SNPs by encoding structural variants and transposable elements as one-hot marker representations.
Introduces NovGMDeep, a four-layer 1D convolutional network with max pooling and dropout, designed for marker counts far larger than the sample size.
Outperforms rrBLUP, gBLUP, DeepGS, and G2Pdeep on Arabidopsis thaliana phenotypes.
Documents where the approach fails: with only 176 rice accessions, deep models lose to statistical baselines.
methods: One-hot encoding of structural variants and transposable elements
Pearson correlation and mean absolute error evaluation
Comparison against rrBLUP, gBLUP, DeepGS, and G2Pdeep
data: Arabidopsis thaliana: 914 accessions with 155,440 structural variant markers, and 923 accessions with SNP markers, from the 1001 Genomes project and the European Variation Archive
Phenotypes from AraPheno: flowering time, rosette leaf number, cauline axillary branch number, stem length
Oryza sativa subsp. Japonica: 176 accessions with 6,074 transposable element markers and 493,882 SNP markers
Rice phenotypes: panicle length, spikelet number, days to heading, plant height
results: Flowering time PCC of 0.788 with structural variants against 0.594 with SNPs
Structural variants beat SNPs on all four Arabidopsis phenotypes and beat both statistical baselines
Mean absolute error roughly halved for structural variants relative to SNPs
Transposable element markers outperformed SNPs in rice, though the small cohort limited deep model performance
applications: Genomic selection and breeding value estimation in crops
Genotype-to-phenotype association beyond SNP markers
Trait prediction for Arabidopsis and rice breeding programs

publications.title: Integument colour change: Tracking delayed growth of Oppia nitens as a sub-lethal indicator of soil toxicity
publications.shortTitle: Mite colour change as a soil toxicity indicator
publications.summary: Turns the colour of a soil mite's shell into a measurable toxicity endpoint. Image analysis of how the integument of Oppia nitens darkens from amber to brown tracks growth, detecting sublethal heavy metal and organic contamination within seven days.
publications.abstract: Growth is an important toxicity end-point in ecotoxicology but is rarely used in soil ecotoxicological studies. Here, we assessed the growth change of Oppia nitens when exposed to reference and heavy metal toxicants. To assess mite growth, we developed an image analysis methodology to measure colour spectrum changes of the mite integument at the final developmental stage, as a proxy for growth change. We linked the values of red, green, blue, key-black, and light colour of mites to different growth stages. Our method of mite colour change detected sublethal effects within seven days of exposure at levels close to those that inhibit reproduction. At sublethal concentrations, cadmium, copper, zinc, phenanthrene and boric acid delayed the growth of Oppia nitens. As expected, cadmium was the most toxic metal on the growth of the mites. Assessing mite growth changes with image analytic methods is a step in the right direction in exploring additional toxicity endpoints.
contributions: Establishes integument colour change from amber to dark brown as a measurable proxy for growth in Oppia nitens.
Develops an image analysis method linking red, green, blue, key-black, and lightness values to developmental stage.
Detects sublethal toxicity within seven days, at concentrations close to those that inhibit reproduction.
Adds growth to the small set of usable endpoints in soil ecotoxicology, alongside survival and reproduction.
data: Oppia nitens exposed to cadmium, copper, zinc, phenanthrene, and boric acid
Colour measurements of the mite integument at the final developmental stage
Growth responses compared against published survival and reproduction endpoints
results: Sublethal growth delay detected within seven days of exposure
Growth was as sensitive an endpoint as reproduction
Cadmium was the most toxic of the metals tested on mite growth
applications: Soil contamination assessment and environmental remediation
Ecotoxicological risk assessment for agricultural soils
Image-based phenotyping of soil invertebrates

datasets.name: WheatSeedBelt
datasets.title: WheatSeedBelt: single-kernel wheat imaging dataset with Fusarium damage annotations
datasets.description: A high-resolution, large-scale dataset of 40,420 close-up top- and side-view single-kernel images covering 268 wheat varieties, annotated for kernel damage including Fusarium damaged kernels. Introduced to support image-based phenotyping of Fusarium head blight resistance where large-scale damage-annotated kernel data did not previously exist.

datasets.name: GWFSS
datasets.title: GWFSS: Global Wheat Full Semantic Organ Segmentation dataset
datasets.description: A multi-institutional benchmark for full semantic segmentation of wheat organs (leaves, stems, spikes) across all developmental stages, assembled by the Global Wheat Dataset Consortium from 11 institutions using a wide range of imaging setups. Version 1.0 includes 1,096 ground-truth labelled images alongside a larger unlabelled collection, distributed via the ETH Research Collection.
